title: Card Flavor Text Style Pack
body:
Governs trading card game and collectible card game flavor text: brief narrative or atmospheric text appearing on game cards.

**Domain Overview:** Flavor text is the smallest unit of world-building in print. It appears beneath the rules text on a game card — typically 100-200 characters, sometimes as few as 40. It does no mechanical work. It exists entirely to make the card feel like part of a world that existed before the game did and will exist after the game ends. The medium is extreme: a novelist uses 80,000 words; flavor text uses fifteen. The compression required is not a constraint to work around — it is the form itself.

**Flavor text fails when it could belong to any card, any world, any moment. It succeeds when it belongs to exactly this card, in exactly this world, at exactly this instant.**

**Reader:** A player holding the card during a game. They have two to three seconds. Flavor text that requires a second reading to understand has failed. Flavor text that lands on the first pass and rewards a second is the gold standard. Each card's flavor text is also part of an aggregate: fifty cards from one set should cohere into a world-state.

**Voice Model:**
- Maximum compression: every word must justify its position. Test every word: if the line still works without it, cut it. The length limit is not the enemy — slack within the limit is.
- One clear image or implication: flavor text that tries to do two things does neither well. One image: the door, the debt, the moment before. Identify the one thing this flavor text adds to the card's identity.
- World-weight: fifteen words should feel like a fragment of something enormous. Achieved not by claiming enormity ('the greatest battle ever fought') but by specificity that implies context. 'She didn't betray the king. She just stopped pretending to serve him.' — this implies a relationship, a decision, a history, without naming any of it.
- The frame is the frame: the art tells one story; the flavor text does not re-describe the art. It adds what the art cannot: a voice, a consequence, a contradiction, a prior moment, a future implication.
- Memorable after one reading: can the player quote it, approximately, an hour later? Achieved through an unexpected word, an unusual structure, or an implication the reader must briefly hold.

**Tone:** Card-specific. Removal spells: dry, surgical, final. Combat spells: kinetic, terse, often from the perspective of the defeated. Dark artifacts: clinical precision implying wrongness ('It works exactly as intended.'). Heroic cards: wry rather than triumphant. Enchantments: mythic, slightly alien. Creature cards: often the creature's voice or a witness's voice.

**Sentence Count:** One sentence strongly preferred. Two sentences permitted only for before/after structure, call-and-response, or tension and resolution. Three sentences is almost always wrong.

**Sentence Structure:** Fragments acceptable and often preferred. No explanatory clauses ('which means that', 'in other words', 'as a result'). Inverted structures used once per card at most for emphasis.

**Quotation Format:** 'Flavor text in quotation marks.' followed by —Speaker name, title or descriptor on a separate line. The speaker should be relevant to the card's mechanic or story moment — not a random wise-sounding sage.

**Narrative Format:** No quotation marks. One or two sentences. Third person or second person. Present tense for immediacy; past tense for historical weight. Never future tense as a statement of fact.

**Character Count Discipline:** Most games impose hard limits of 140-200 characters including spaces and attribution. Write to fit. Count characters before finalizing.

**Preferred Vocabulary:** Unusual specific nouns with world-weight ('the debt', 'the third bell', 'the surveyor's mark'); active verbs that do work (holds, forgets, costs, waits, breaks); strong monosyllabic words (debt, scar, dusk, spent, lock); invented world-terms used without definition when evocative and comprehensible by feel.

**Forbidden Vocabulary:** ancient, mystical, powerful, legendary, sacred (empty modifier adjectives unless the line can keep the promise); simile constructions ('like a river that...', 'as cold as...'); overlong conjunctions and subordination; generic epic sentiment ('For glory! For the realm!'); dialogue tags on attributed quotes.

**Anti-Patterns:** Explaining what the card does mechanically; generic epic sentiment; too many syllables destroying the rhythm; flavor that could belong to any card; the obvious reading (restating what the art already shows); hedging and qualification ('it was said that perhaps...').
